Mental Health Care Plan

Patient & GP Details
- Patient: Name: Tim (conflict noted — patient later addressed as "Kim" in transcript), DOB: Not recorded, Gender: Not explicitly recorded (patient reports Implanon contraceptive; gender inference uncertain — conflict/uncertainty noted), Contact: Not recorded, Address: Not recorded
- Referring GP: Not recorded. Practice: Not recorded. Practice Address: Not recorded. Provider No.: Not recorded. Contact: Not recorded

Clinical Assessment

Identified Problems/Provisional Diagnoses:
- Principal: Suspected acute lower urinary tract infection (cystitis) — high likelihood (empirically treated by clinician; consistent with DDx)
- Secondary: Urolithiasis (ureteric/bladder stone) — medium likelihood (DDx)
- Tertiary: Gynecologic causes (ectopic pregnancy, ovarian cyst/ovarian torsion) — medium likelihood (DDx)
(DDx items included above are those consistent with the transcript and differential reasoning.)

Clinical Details & History:
- Medications: Implanon contraceptive (inserted ~1 year ago). Trimethoprim prescribed: "two tablets, one tablet twice a day for 3 days" (dose in mg not documented; route not explicitly stated). Paracetamol advised as needed (dose/route/frequency not documented).

- Smoking/Substance Use: Non-smoker; other substance use not recorded
- Key Stressors: Not recorded

Mental Status Examination (MSE):
- Appearance & General Behaviour: Cooperative, conversational, ambulatory; reports able to move and function despite pain
- Mood & Affect: Not recorded

Cognition:

Risk Assessment:
- Suicidal/Self-Harm/Risk to Others: Not recorded
- Protective Factors: Engaged with healthcare, has social contacts/roommates, employed
- Overall Current Risk Level (Self): Not recorded
- Emergency Contact: Not recorded

Formulation:
- Presenting problem is acute lower central abdominal (suprapubic) pain of 2 days' duration with suprapubic tenderness, subjective feverishness (hot/sweaty), mild nausea, urinary frequency and reported pink-coloured urine.
- Predisposing factors: None documented.
- Precipitating factors: Recent onset (~2 days) of suprapubic pain and possible urinary abnormality.
- Perpetuating factors: Uncertainty regarding cause, no diagnostic test results available yet.
- Protective factors: Prompt presentation to primary care, clinician arranged empiric antibiotic therapy and advised diagnostic testing; social support and employment.
- Psychological/mental health contribution: No documented primary mental health disorder; patient shows transient distress related to acute physical symptoms and uncertainty.

Mental Health Care Plan Details

Principal Problem: Suspected acute lower urinary tract infection (cystitis)
- Patient Goal(s): Resolution of lower abdominal pain and urinary symptoms; avoid complications; confirm pregnancy status if applicable.
- Clinical Goal(s): Empirical treatment of likely UTI, obtain diagnostic tests (urine analysis/culture and pregnancy test), monitor for improvement or deterioration, escalate care if not improving/worsening.
- Actions (Patient):
  - Start prescribed antibiotics (trimethoprim as sent to pharmacy per clinician instruction).
  - Perform a pregnancy test as advised.
  - Take paracetamol for analgesia as suggested.
  - Maintain hydration; consider cranberry juice as discussed.
  - Return to GP or seek urgent care if symptoms worsen (increasing pain, fever, vomiting, syncope) or do not improve in a few days.
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  - Empiric antibiotic prescription sent to pharmacy (Trimethoprim: two tablets, one tablet twice daily for 3 days; mg not documented).
  - Arrange urine testing (urinalysis/urine dipstick and culture) and pregnancy test to clarify diagnosis.
  - Provide safety-netting advice and request review in a few days if not improving or sooner if worsening.
  - Advise analgesia (paracetamol) and hydration.

Secondary Problem: Possible urolithiasis or gynecologic pathology (medium likelihood)
- Patient Goal(s): Identify or exclude stone or gynecologic causes; prevent complications.
- Clinical Goal(s): Arrange appropriate imaging or specialist referral if indicated by test results or clinical deterioration.
- Actions (Patient):
  - Report any escalation in pain severity, new flank pain, syncope, heavy vaginal bleeding, or hemodynamic symptoms immediately to clinician or ED.
  - Attend arranged investigations (urine tests, pregnancy test) and follow-up appointments.
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  - If urine testing is non-diagnostic or red flags present (severe/worsening pain, hemodynamic instability, suspected ectopic pregnancy), arrange urgent pelvic ultrasound and/or abdominal imaging and consider gynaecology/urology referral or ED transfer.
  - Reassess diagnosis after test results and modify treatment accordingly.

Patient Education, Emergency Care & Relapse Prevention:
- Education Given: Yes. Topics Covered: likely causes (UTI, stone, gynecologic causes), need for urine testing and pregnancy test, rationale for empiric antibiotics, analgesia and fluid advice, warning signs prompting urgent review.
- Early Warning Signs of Relapse/Worsening: Increasing or worsening abdominal pain, persistent or worsening fever/subjective hot sweats, vomiting, syncope/lightheadedness, heavy vaginal bleeding, inability to tolerate oral intake.
- Coping Strategies: Use prescribed analgesia (paracetamol), maintain hydration, rest, seek prompt medical review if symptoms worsen.

Consent, Coordination & Review:
- Patient Consent to Plan: Yes — patient verbally agreed to plan in consultation ("I'm happy with that plan.")
- Copy of Mental Health Care Plan Given to Patient: Not recorded
- Other Mental Health Professionals Involved in Patient Care: Not recorded
- GP Acknowledgment (if completed by other MH Professional): Not recorded
- Review Date: Return to GP in a few days for review if not improving; sooner if worsening (exact date/time not documented)

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)
- Acute lower urinary tract infection (cystitis) — Likelihood: High. Justification: Suprapubic burning pain/tenderness, increased urinary frequency, pink-coloured urine; clinician empirically treated for UTI.
- Urolithiasis (ureteric/bladder stone) — Likelihood: Medium. Justification: Hematuria (pink urine) and lower abdominal pain can indicate stone disease; pain character less typical for colic.
- Gynecologic cause (ectopic pregnancy, ovarian cyst/rupture/ torsion) — Likelihood: Medium. Justification: Lower pelvic pain, possible bleeding; pregnancy-related causes remain possible despite Implanon.

Quality checks
● Missing but clinically expected elements: Formal mental health diagnosis (none documented), comprehensive MSE items (orientation, mood, affect), formal risk assessment details (suicidal ideation/self-harm risk), vital signs, urine and pregnancy test results, imaging results, GP/referring provider details, patient DOB/contact/address.
● Internal conflicts between transcript and DDx: Patient name inconsistency in transcript (addressed as "Tim" and later "Kim") — conflict noted. Gender not explicitly recorded though Implanon use suggests female — uncertainty noted.
● Transcript quality notes: Consultation focused on acute physical symptoms; short primary-care visit with limited examination documentation and no vitals or test results recorded. Some minor inconsistencies in patient name used by clinician.
